A standardized toolkit can make results comparable only if the underlying tasks and scores measure legal ability that matters in practice. The web interface lowers friction, but it does not by itself guarantee legal validity or expert agreement. Acceleration backends and recoverable pipelines improve practical experimentation, but they do not remove model bias, hallucinated legal reasoning, or weak benchmark design. The toolkit also depends on community adoption: transparency and comparability matter most when many researchers actually use the same conventions and document their settings clearly.

368.bp: Starlink is no longer just a space project. It is part of the everyday Internet path for people, businesses, ships, disaster zones, and remote places that may not have good ground cables. But the part of Starlink that touches the public Internet is not only satellites in orbit. There is also a ground-side system of private networks, public addresses, naming records, user traffic, and services that must be operated securely. The paper asks how outsiders can understand that system when the operator does not publish a full map. Its answer is to treat DNS, the Internet's name lookup system, as a source of indirect evidence. When machines ask for names or when records mention internal hosts, those traces can reveal structure. The practical need is external measurement: learning how a major Internet infrastructure is organized, used, and exposed without relying on private disclosure.
368.wh: The difficulty is that Starlink's most important ground-side details are partly hidden by design. A private network is supposed to be private, user activity is scattered across many lookups, and public IP addresses can belong to infrastructure or to end users. Looking at only one window gives a distorted view. Internal DNS leakage may hint at private network structure, but leakage alone does not say how people use the network. Passive DNS can show name lookup patterns over time, but it may mix ordinary user behavior with operator services. Active scanning can reveal exposed services, but scanning the wrong addresses could confuse customer devices with Starlink-operated systems. The central tension is visibility versus interpretation. The researchers can observe traces, not walk inside the network. They must decide which traces belong together, which addresses represent infrastructure, and which observed services matter for security.
368.naive: A smart beginner might start by collecting Starlink IP ranges and scanning every address for open services. That sounds direct: if a port answers, record it; if many ports answer, call it risky. The plan fails because public address space can include both infrastructure-related machines and end-user endpoints, so the result may blame Starlink operations for things that are really customer-side. Another beginner might only inspect public DNS records, but public records can miss private naming habits and internal structure. A third might only watch passive DNS queries, yet usage trends do not by themselves identify vulnerable exposed services. The simple approaches each see one kind of clue and then overread it.
368.ap: The core idea is multi-perspective measurement. Instead of trusting one trace, the paper combines three DNS-centered views. First, it uses internal DNS leakage, meaning name information that appears to reveal private Starlink network structure, to infer how parts of the private network may be organized. Second, it analyzes passive DNS data, which records observed name lookup activity without directly probing the target, to describe user behavior patterns and service usage trends. Third, it actively scans Starlink's IP address space to see what services are reachable and what that implies about the security posture. DNS records are also used as a filter: they help separate infrastructure-related IPs from end-user IPs before judging service deployment. The central move is not that DNS gives a perfect map. It is that DNS supplies labels and repeated traces that make scanning and behavior measurement less blind.
368.mech: The mechanism begins with the paper's object of study: Starlink's terrestrial network, meaning the ground-side ecosystem where satellite service connects into the Internet. The first input is DNS leakage. DNS normally translates names into network addresses, but names can contain hints about internal machines, regions, roles, or private address structure. The researchers collect such leakage and group the clues to infer the shape of Starlink's private networks. The second input is passive DNS data. Here the system does not need to touch Starlink machines directly; it studies recorded lookup activity to see what names are being resolved and how those patterns change. From this, it identifies user behavior patterns and service usage trends, staying at the level supported by DNS traces rather than claiming direct access to user content. The third input is Starlink IP address space for active scanning. The scan asks which services answer from reachable addresses. Before interpreting those answers, DNS records help isolate infrastructure-related IPs from addresses more likely tied to end users. The outputs are three linked descriptions: a possible internal network structure, a picture of service and user activity from passive lookups, and an assessment of exposed services and security posture from scanning.
368.math: The main mathematical idea is inference from indirect traces. Inference means starting with observations that are incomplete and asking what hidden structure would make those observations make sense. Here the observations are DNS names, DNS lookup histories, IP addresses, and scan responses. The hidden objects are private network organization, service deployment, user behavior patterns, and security exposure. A second idea is classification: deciding whether an IP address should be treated as infrastructure-related or end-user-related. That decision matters because the same scan result has different meaning depending on who owns the machine being scanned. A third idea is aggregation over repeated events. One DNS query is a weak clue; many queries over time can reveal trends because repeated observations smooth out one-off noise. There is also graph-like reasoning, although the abstract does not name a graph method: names point to addresses, addresses answer with services, and repeated links between these objects let evidence travel. The tradeoff is detail versus reliability. DNS compresses rich network behavior into names and lookups, so it loses packet-level context, but it gains broad coverage and repeated evidence.
368.dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader measurement and security work: it studies a deployed web infrastructure from the outside and turns public or leaked traces into evidence about hidden operation. It also connects to retrieval and ranking ideas because the researchers must select the right clues from a large pile of DNS records and IP responses, then decide which ones are relevant to infrastructure rather than users. It connects to graph reasoning because DNS naturally links names, addresses, services, and organizational roles; the meaning comes from relationships among those objects, not from one record alone. In the repo's current JSON data, another nearby satellite paper studies Starlink and Kuiper as low-Earth-orbit networks supporting web services under space radiation. That sibling concern is resilience during operation. This paper's concern is visibility: how to map architecture, usage, and exposure when the system is large, important, and externally opaque.
368.ww: The approach should work better than a single-view study because each view corrects a weakness in the others. Internal DNS leakage is valuable because private names can reveal organization that public service banners cannot. But leakage may be partial, so passive DNS adds repeated evidence about which services are actually looked up and how usage appears over time. Passive DNS, in turn, does not prove which services are exposed to the network, so active scanning asks reachable machines directly what they run. The DNS-based separation between infrastructure IPs and end-user IPs is especially important. Without that separation, scanning results could mix operator-managed service deployment with customer behavior and produce a misleading security picture. The intuitive reason is triangulation: when several imperfect clues point toward the same structure, the conclusion is more credible than when one clue is stretched too far. DNS is a good anchor because naming is required for ordinary Internet use, so it leaves operational traces even when the full internal map is hidden.
368.po: The payoff is an external characterization of Starlink's ground-side network ecosystem. Grounded in the abstract, the paper provides insight into private network architecture through internal DNS leakage, user behavior and service usage trends through passive DNS, and service deployment plus security posture through large-scale active scanning. It also buys a cleaner measurement method by using DNS records to distinguish infrastructure-related IPs from end-user IPs. In practical terms, the work gives researchers, operators, and security observers a way to discuss a major satellite Internet provider using measured evidence rather than speculation.
368.limits: The claims depend on DNS traces being representative enough to support inference. If leakage is incomplete or misleading, the private network picture may be partial. Passive DNS only captures observed lookup behavior, not all user activity or payload content. Active scanning shows services that answer during the scan window, so it can miss temporary services, filtered addresses, or behavior that changes by location. The infrastructure-versus-end-user separation relies on DNS records being accurate labels. The abstract says the findings provide insights, but it does not prove a complete Starlink map, a full vulnerability audit, or causal explanations for user behavior trends.

369.bp: Chinese idioms are like colorful sayings in English ('raining cats and dogs')—the literal words (cats, dogs) don't explain the real meaning (heavy rain). Multimodal systems need to get this: the picture and text together should point to the idiom's true metaphorical sense, not just its surface words.
369.wh: An idiom's literal words and true meaning can be opposite. 'Kill two birds with one stone' sounds violent but means efficiency. Worse, the same idiom means different things in different contexts. Systems that just match words to images miss the metaphor entirely.
369.ap: The system builds a graph showing explicit relationships between literal and metaphorical meanings of each idiom. It also creates specialized sub-systems (experts) that understand different types of idioms—one for when literal and metaphorical meanings apply, one for when they diverge. Each expert focuses on its specialty; they vote to pick the best idiom.
369.ww: Explicit semantic graphs make metaphors tangible rather than hidden. Specialized experts divide the labor, so the system doesn't try to solve all idiom types the same way. Voting combines their knowledge.
369.po: System accurately selects idioms from image-text pairs, handling both the literal-to-metaphorical jump and context-dependent meanings better than systems that ignore metaphor.

370.bp: Language models now augment their answers by fetching real data from knowledge bases before answering. This is safer than hallucination—if the data is trustworthy. But what if attackers slip false information into the knowledge base? Systems need defenses.
370.wh: Graph-based knowledge systems reorganize raw text into structured graphs (entities, relationships) before retrieval. This should be safer than raw-text systems because structure filters noise. But attackers can also forge structure—fake relations, fake entities that look real—and mislead the model.
370.ap: The attacker creates poisoned 'toxic events' (fake facts disguised as real ones) and plants them in the knowledge base. They also fake the history of how these facts evolved from real information, making false knowledge seem like it legitimately evolved from seed facts. In multi-target attacks, they link poisons so they reinforce each other.
370.ww: Structured graphs look more trustworthy to models, so poisoned structure is more persuasive than raw text. Fake event evolution (showing false intermediate steps) makes invented facts seem like natural consequences of real knowledge.
370.po: Demonstrates vulnerabilities in graph-based knowledge systems; shows attackers can poison knowledge graphs more effectively than raw-text systems, revealing a security gap in retrieval-augmented systems.

371.bp: Graph neural networks learn from network structure (social graphs, citation graphs, molecule connections). Most treat the whole graph as one flat object. But real graphs hide internal organization—tight communities, bottleneck nodes—that matter for learning.
371.wh: Treating a graph as flat misses its internal structure. Some nodes act as bridges between communities; some are local hubs. Simple augmentation (randomly removing nodes) treats all removals equally, but destroying a bridge is much worse than removing a hub.
371.ap: Decompose the graph into tree-like structures (a classical graph theory tool) where local neighborhoods become 'bags.' Compute importance scores for each node and edge based on their role as bridges or hubs. Use these scores to make intelligent augmentation: preserve bridges, destroy isolated nodes, weaken global hubs. Also craft a new similarity loss that treats tree-based proximity differently from plain graph distance.
371.ww: Decomposition reveals hidden structure. Importance scores target augmentation intelligently—removing what matters most (bridges) hurts learning worse than random, so preserving them matters. Tree-based similarity captures topology that edge-based distance alone misses.
371.po: Graph learning (self-supervised and supervised) improves over state-of-the-art by respecting internal structure during augmentation and similarity computation.

372.bp: VTubers—digital avatars with human performers—are a multi-billion-dollar entertainment industry. But the business model is punishing: agencies own the persona, the performer bears all reputational risk, and when they quit and restart ('reincarnation'), they lose audience, income, and sometimes face harassment.
372.wh: Nobody has measured the cost of reincarnation at scale. Is it a minor blip or catastrophic? Without numbers, performers and agencies can't push for better contracts or industry reform.
372.ap: Researchers analyzed 12 major reincarnation cases using 728K livestream sessions and 4.5 billion viewer interactions, tracking metrics like audience size, revenue, harassment, and industry impact before and after reincarnation.
372.ww: Large-scale data reveals patterns individual cases might hide. Livestream metrics are objective (viewers can't lie), and social media interactions capture harassment quantitatively.
372.po: First empirical study proving reincarnation causes severe career damage to performers—substantial audience loss, income drop, increased harassment—with implications for labor practices and industry sustainability.

373.bp: Graph classification systems are trained on a fixed set of categories (e.g., 'toxic', 'safe'). But in the real world, new node types appear that the model never saw (novel classes). The system must either classify unknown nodes or reject them as 'unknown,' without retraining.
373.wh: Standard graph learning maximizes performance on known classes but doesn't build clear boundaries between known and unknown. Novel class nodes cluster randomly among known classes instead of being recognized as outliers. Existing methods don't handle mixing known and novel classes well.
373.ap: Novel 'negative Mixup' synthetically creates intermediate examples between known classes that push the model to learn clearer decision boundaries. Separate contrastive learning (training examples to be similar to their true class, different from others) maximizes spread between classes and compactness within classes, across multiple graph-processing layers.
373.ww: Negative Mixup creates hard cases at class boundaries, forcing the decision boundary to be clear and sharp rather than fuzzy. Multi-layer contrastive learning ensures that structure (how nodes connect) is consistent with class identity at every depth, making unknown nodes stand out as poorly-connected-to-any-class.
373.po: System reliably rejects novel class nodes while maintaining high accuracy on known classes, even when test data heavily mixes known and unknown categories.

374.bp: Live streaming platforms need real-time moderation and sentiment detection—flagging hate speech or sudden mood shifts instantly. But video, audio, and text streams arrive asynchronously and late, so systems must decide with partial information.
374.wh: The lightweight encoder learns by aligning audio/visual cues with text (cross-modal contrastive training). Loss down-weights examples where the target segment barely overlaps the frame, since those cases are too noisy to learn from reliably.
374.ap: Use a fast, lightweight streaming encoder for most frames. When a case is ambiguous or needs deeper understanding, route it to a heavyweight vision-language model. If context is insufficient (too early in a scene), defer the decision until more evidence arrives.
374.po: System achieves accuracy comparable to using vision-language models alone while calling the expensive model only occasionally, dramatically reducing latency and computation on live streams.
